<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par126 />(''b'') With a title understood and recognized by every one, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַמֶּ֫לֶךְ שְׁלֹמהֹ}} ὁ βασιλεὺς Σαλωμών: {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=35|verse=8}} ''under the oak'' (the well-known oak which was there).

(''c'') With appellatives to denote persons or natural objects which are unique, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=הַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדוֹל|translate=the high priest}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַשֶּׁ֫מֶשׁ|translate=the sun}}, {{GHGheb|text=הָאָ֫רֶץ|translate=the earth}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|126|e}}
(''d'') When terms applying to whole classes are restricted (simply by usage) to particular individuals (like ὁ ποιητής, meaning Homer) or things, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שָׂטָן|translate=adversary}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַשָּׂטָן|translate=the adversary, Satan}}; {{GHGheb|text=בַּ֫עַל|translate=lord}}, {{GHGheb|text=הַבַּ֫עַל|translate=Baal}} as proper name of the god; {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאָדָם|translate=the}} (first) ''man, Adam''; {{GHGheb|text=הָאֱלֹהִים}}<ref>On the subsequent change of {{GHGheb|text=שָׂטָן}}, {{GHGheb|text=אָדָם}}, {{GHGheb|text=אֱלֹהִים}} into real proper names by the omission of the article, cf. above, {{GHGpar|125|f}}.</ref> or {{GHGheb|text=הָאֵל}} ὁ θεός, ''the one true God'' (cf. also ὁ Χριστός in the New Testament); also {{GHGheb|text=הַנָּהָר|translate=the river}}, i.e. ''Euphrates''; {{GHGheb|text=הַכִּכָּר|translate=the circle}}, sc. of the Jordan, ''the Jordan plain'' [{{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=17}}, &c.].

(''e'') Very often with the vocative, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=14|verse=4}} {{GHGheb|text=הוֹשִׁ֫עָה הַמֶּ֫לֶךְ|translate=help, O king}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=3|verse=8}} {{GHGheb|text=יְהוֹשֻׁעַ הַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדוֹל|translate=O Joshua the high priest}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=58}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=24|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=9|verse=5}}; in the plural, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=2}}, 13; but cf. also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=10|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=49|verse=13|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=שָׁמַ֫יִם}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫רֶץ}}); 23:16, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ho|chapter=13|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=1|verse=5}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=34|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=10|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=11|verse=9|hidebook=1}}, &c.<ref>For further exceptions see Nestle, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZAW.|Zeitschrift für die alttestamentliche Wissenschaft, ed. by B. Stade, Giessen, 1881 ff., and since 1907 by K. Marti.}}}} 1904, p. 323 ff.</ref> The vocative occurs ''without'' the article in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=22|verse=2}}, since it has been already defined by a preceding accusative.

{{GHGmargin-letter|126|f}}
Rem. Strictly speaking in all these cases the substantive with the article is really in apposition to the personal pronoun of the 2nd person, which is either expressly mentioned or virtually present (in the imperative), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=17|verse=58}} ''thou, the young man''. But such passages as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=42|verse=18}}, where the vocative precedes the imperative, prove that in such cases the substantive originally in apposition eventually acquired the value of a complete clause.

{{GHGmargin-letter|126|g}}
(''f'') With words denoting classes (see particulars under l).

(''g'') In a peculiar way, to specify persons or things, which are so far definite as to be naturally thought of in connexion with a given case, and must be assumed accordingly to be there (see q–s).

(''h'') With adjectives (also ordinal numbers and demonstrative pronouns used adjectivally) which are joined to substantives determined in some way (see u).

{{GHGmargin-letter|126|h}}
Rem. The article may be omitted in ''poetry'' in all the above-mentioned cases; in general it is used in poetry far less frequently than in prose. Its use or omission probably often rests on rhythmical grounds;<ref>Cf. the useful statistics of J. Ley in the {{GHGcite|title=Neue Jahrbücher für Philologie und Pädagogik}}, 2te Abteilung, 1891, Heft 7–9, and M. Lambert, ‘ ''L’article dans la po&ésie hébr.'',’ {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|REJ.|Revue des Études Juives. Paris, 1880 ff.}}}} 37, 263 ff.</ref> it is sometimes omitted also for rhetorical reasons. Cf. e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫רֶץ}} for {{GHGheb|text=הָאָ֫רֶץ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=2}}; {{GHGheb|text=מְלָכִים}} as vocative, verse 10; {{GHGheb|text=מֶ֫לֶךְ}} for {{GHGheb|text=הַמֶּ֫לֶךְ}} 21:2; {{GHGheb|text=שִׁמְךָ גָּדוֹל וְנוֹרָא}} (contrary to ''u, v'') 99:3. In the instances in which the {{GHGheb|text=ה}} of the article is omitted after a prefix ({{GHGpar|35|n}}), the vowel of the article is often retained after the prefix even in poetry, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=בַּשָּׁמַ֫יִם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=4}}, &c.
